segments.english: Now the men of Sodom were wicked and sinners against the LORD, exceedingly.
segments.literal: and-men-of Sodom wicked and-sinners to-the-LORD exceedingly

tokens.note: construct plural of אִישׁ; the vav is circumstantial or contrastive: 'now'
adjective; predicate with no verb 'to be' written
ל with יהוה: 'in relation to the LORD', 'against'
the noun מְאֹד used as an adverb

phrases.literal: 'and-men-of Sodom'; the vav marks a new circumstance after the separation of Abram and Lot

grammar: The verse is a verbless clause: subject אַנְשֵׁי סְדֹם, predicates רָעִים and חַטָּאִים.
The etnaḥta falls on וְחַטָּאִים, so לַיהוָה מְאֹד is read as a closing phrase that intensifies both predicates.
מְאֹד is a noun used adverbially, 'exceedingly'.
segments.note: The adjectives are kept apart, 'wicked' and 'sinners', because Rashi and Ibn Ezra distinguish them: wicked toward people, sinning against the LORD. 'Against' renders ל as the context requires.

commentary.summary: Rashi: even so, Lot did not refrain from living among them; the rabbis learn from here 'the name of the wicked rots' (Prov 10:7). This is a comment on Lot, not on the words.
Rashi: רעים בגופם, wicked in their bodies, that is in their persons. The English keeps 'wicked' and the note records the sense.
Rashi: וחטאים במלונם, sinners in their wealth (Sanhedrin 109). This distinguishes the two terms; the English keeps them separate.
Rashi: they knew their Master and intended to rebel against Him. This supports 'sinners against the LORD, exceedingly' as deliberate sin.
Ibn Ezra: רעים is said of people, and compares Ezekiel 16:49, 'they did not strengthen the hand of the poor and needy'. So 'wicked' is toward other people, and 'sinners' toward the LORD.
Radak: wicked toward heaven and toward people, all of it sin against the LORD, since they broke the commandments given to Adam and Noah.
Ramban: the verse blames Lot for living among them, and also shows the merit of the righteous, since the cities of the plain were destroyed.

apparatus: 13:13.5 vowels: WLC reads לַיהוָה; the base text has לַיהֹוָה. The English is the same.
Onkelos: wicked 'in their wealth' and guilty 'in their bodies'; the reverse of Rashi's distribution.

segments.english: The LORD said to Abram, after Lot had separated from him, "Lift your eyes and look from the place where you are, northward and southward and eastward and westward."
segments.literal: and-the-LORD said to Abram after being-separated Lot from-with-him lift please your-eyes and-see from-the-place which you there northward and-southward and-eastward and-westward

tokens.note: וַ before יהוה: a vav in sequence with the preceding narrative
qatal after a fronted subject: past perfect sense is possible, 'had said'
nifal infinitive construct with a subject: 'after Lot's being separated'
מֵעִם 'from beside', with the 3ms suffix
idiom: שָׂא עֵינַיִם 'lift the eyes', look up
particle of exhortation; softens the command
dual construct with 2ms suffix
directional he: 'toward the north'
directional he; נֶגֶב is 'south' (the Negev)
directional he; קֶדֶם 'east'
directional he; יָם 'sea', hence 'west'

phrases.english: after Lot had separated from him
phrases.literal: 'after being-separated Lot from-with-him'; the infinitive gives a time clause
'lift please your-eyes'; נָא is not rendered in the English

phrases.english: from the place where you are
phrases.literal: 'from-the-place which you there'; the verbless relative clause is read 'where you are'

phrases.english: northward and southward and eastward and westward

grammar: The clause opens with וַיהוָה אָמַר, a fronted subject and a qatal, so it reads as background: the LORD had spoken, or spoke, once Lot was gone.
אַחֲרֵי הִפָּרֶד־לוֹט is a preposition with an infinitive construct and its subject.
שָׂא נָא עֵינֶיךָ וּרְאֵה: two imperatives; נָא makes the command a request.
Each of the four directions takes the directional ה, 'toward'; the sea is the west because the Mediterranean lies there.
segments.note: The perfect after a fronted subject is rendered as a simple past with 'after' carrying the order. The omitted נָא is recorded in the phrase note.

commentary.summary: Rashi: as long as the wicked man was with him, the divine word held back from him. This fits the English, which puts the speech after the separation.
Radak: Abram might have thought Lot also had a share in the land; now that Lot has left he is told that it is for Abram and his seed alone.
Sforno: this was not said while Lot was with him, lest Lot and his shepherds grow proud and seize it.

apparatus: 13:14.1 vowels: WLC reads וַיהוָה; the base text has וַיהֹוָה.

segments.english: for all the land that you see I will give to you and to your offspring forever.
segments.literal: for [object-mark] all-the-land which you seeing to-you I-will-give-it and-to-your-seed until forever

tokens.note: 'the land' as a whole, in the sense of the land of Canaan
active participle: 'you are seeing'
fronted for emphasis: 'to you, and to no one else'
yiqtol with a 3fs object suffix; the doubled nun is the energic form
זֶרַע is collective: 'seed', 'descendants'
עוֹלָם 'long duration'; with עַד, 'to a distant time'

phrases.literal: 'which you seeing'; a participle with a pronoun
'to-you I-will-give-it'; the English puts the pronoun after the verb and omits the suffix 'it' since the object is already stated

grammar: The object, כָּל־הָאָרֶץ, comes first, then the relative clause, then the verb, so the whole land is stressed.
אֶתְּנֶנָּה has a nun-energic suffix, a resumptive pronoun for the fronted object.
רֹאֶה is a participle: the land is what Abram is looking at.
The etnaḥta falls on אֶתְּנֶנָּה, so וּלְזַרְעֲךָ עַד־עוֹלָם is a second clause.
segments.note: The resumptive suffix on אֶתְּנֶנָּה is not repeated in English because the fronted object already stands in the sentence.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: לך אתננה is 'in speech', that is, the gift is made by the word; he compares 'and he shall put them on the head of the goat' (Lev 16:21). So 'I will give' is a promise already made, not yet fulfilled.
Radak: though Abram could not see it all, he saw its four sides, and as it is within its boundaries so it will be given.
Radak: even if they are exiled from it, they will in the end return to it. This reads עד עולם as 'in the end' rather than strict perpetuity.

segments.english: I will make your offspring like the dust of the earth, so that if anyone can count the dust of the earth, then your offspring too can be counted.
segments.literal: and-I-will-set [object-mark] your-seed like-dust-of the-earth which if is-able man to-count [object-mark] dust-of the-earth also your-seed will-be-counted

tokens.note: weqatal continuing the promise: a future
אֲשֶׁר with אִם: 'so that if', a result clause
infinitive construct with ל, complement of יוּכַל
nifal imperfect; a modal sense, 'can be counted'

phrases.english: like the dust of the earth
so that if anyone can count
phrases.literal: 'which if is-able man to-count'; אֲשֶׁר אִם is 'such that if'

phrases.english: then your offspring too can be counted
phrases.literal: 'also your-seed will-be-counted'; the second half of the conditional

grammar: כַּעֲפַר הָאָרֶץ is a simile of number, not of substance.
אֲשֶׁר אִם introduces a conditional with a result sense: 'such that if ...'.
The apodosis גַּם־זַרְעֲךָ יִמָּנֶה has no particle of its own; גַּם marks the parallel.
The wordplay on the root מנה: יוּכַל ... לִמְנוֹת, then יִמָּנֶה.
segments.note: 'Dust' is the plain sense of עָפָר here; the verb שַׂמְתִּי is rendered 'make' in the sense 'turn into', as in 'make a nation'.

commentary.summary: Rashi: just as it is impossible for the dust to be counted, so your seed will not be counted. This is the English's reading of the conditional.
Radak: a hyperbole, as in 'like the sand of the sea and the stars of heaven' (Gen 22:17); the midrash applies the dust to Israel when it does not do His will and the stars when it does.
Radak: if this can be, so can that; that is, since the first is impossible so is the second. He compares Jer 13:23.

apparatus: The sentence has a pause at ׀ after אֲשֶׁר (legarmeh in the base text); the reading follows the zaqef qaton after הָאָרֶץ.

segments.english: Get up, walk about the land through its length and its breadth, for I will give it to you.
segments.literal: arise walk-about in-the-land to-its-length and-to-its-breadth for to-you I-will-give-it

tokens.note: the imperative is auxiliary: 'get up and ...'
hitpael imperative: repeated, to-and-fro walking
construct form with a 3fs suffix
construct form with a 3fs suffix

phrases.literal: 'in-the-land'; the preposition is absorbed by 'walk about'

phrases.english: through its length and its breadth
I will give it to you

grammar: קוּם הִתְהַלֵּךְ: a pair of imperatives; the first is a preliminary, 'get going'.
The hitpael of הלך gives the sense 'walk back and forth'.
The distributive ל on אָרְכָּהּ and רָחְבָּהּ is 'along'.
The etnaḥta on וּלְרָחְבָּהּ divides the command from its reason.
segments.note: The land is the object of 'walk about'; the preposition ב means 'in' or 'through'.

commentary.summary: Ramban: this may be a permission, to go where he likes under divine protection, or a command to take possession by walking; the plain sense is that he would rule in the land wherever he went.
Radak: its length means east to west.
Radak: its breadth means north to south.
Sforno: even in Abram's days he would be a prince of God in the eyes of the inhabitants (Gen 23:6).

segments.english: Abram moved his tent, came and settled at the oaks of Mamre, which are in Hebron, and built there an altar to the LORD.
segments.literal: and-pitched-tent Abram and-came and-dwelt in-oaks-of Mamre which in-Hebron and-built there altar to-the-LORD

tokens.note: denominative verb from אֹהֶל 'tent': 'pitch a tent, move a tent'; the stem is Qal in the parse, though BDB lists the sense under Pi
wayyiqtol
wayyiqtol of ישב: 'dwell'
plural construct of אֵלוֹן 'terebinth'; the trees are often called 'oaks' or 'terebinths'

grammar: Four wayyiqtols in a row (וַיֶּאֱהַל, וַיָּבֹא, וַיֵּשֶׁב, וַיִּבֶן) give the narrative sequence of Abram's move.
בְּאֵלֹנֵי מַמְרֵא: a construct chain; Mamre is a personal name, not a place.
אֲשֶׁר בְּחֶבְרוֹן is a verbless relative clause on the oaks.
The paragraph mark פ closes the unit.
segments.note: I follow Rashi and Ibn Ezra on Mamre, taking it as a man's name and the oaks as the oaks in Hebron. The Hebrew verb is intransitive: 'he pitched tent', so 'moved his tent' is an interpretive rendering.

commentary.summary: Rashi: מַמְרֵא is a man's name. So the English says 'the oaks of Mamre' as 'Mamre's oaks'.
Ibn Ezra: here he explains that the oaks of Mamre are in Hebron. The English reads אֲשֶׁר בְּחֶבְרוֹן as modifying the oaks.
Radak: these are not the oak of Moreh (Gen 12:6); there were two or more plains belonging to a man called Mamre, brother of Eshkol and Aner.
Radak: he took up his tent from there and pitched it from place to place until he arrived.
Sforno: he set his livestock's tents in order here and there.

apparatus: 13:18.12 vowels: WLC reads לַיהוָה; the base text has לַיהֹוָה.
Onkelos renders אֵלֹנֵי as 'plains' (מֵישְׁרֵי) rather than 'oaks'.
